title: What should you ask first in a competitive response case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in a competitive response case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: When a rival makes a move, the client wants to know how to respond. Here is how to keep your head and give a balanced answer.
body:
The first question to ask

How big is the threat in revenue terms?

How to build your structure

  • Exposure (customers, revenue and margin at risk)
  • Rival's motive (segments targeted, can they keep it up)
  • Options (do nothing, defend current customers, respond on price or product, partner or buy)
  • Choose on impact, cost, speed and risk vs doing nothing

The trap most people fall into

Not comparing to doing nothing.

For the full tree, with every branch, read the competitive response framework.

Worked response: a competitor discounts by 20%

A coffee brand sells 1 million packs at £5 each, with £3 variable cost per pack. Contribution is £2 million. A rival launches at £4, and management wants to match the price immediately. Matching would reduce contribution to £1 per pack. Even if the brand retained all its volume, contribution would halve to £1 million.

First determine exposure: which customers would actually switch, in which stores, and what makes them price-sensitive? Ask whether the competitor's discount is temporary or can be sustained. Then compare options: targeted loyalty offers for vulnerable shoppers, a smaller pack at a lower shelf price, product differentiation, selective matching, or no response in less-exposed channels.

The decision depends on expected profit under each option. For example, if holding price loses 20% of volume, contribution becomes 800,000 × £2 = £1.6 million, still higher than matching price at unchanged volume. Include reactions from retailers and competitors before choosing. Doing nothing is a real option that deserves calculation.
